content: To determine whether individuals aged 65 and older respond differently to erythromycin compared to younger subjects, it is essential to include a sufficient number of elderly participants in clinical studies. However, other reported clinical experiences have not identified significant differences in responses between elderly and younger patients. When prescribing erythromycin to elderly patients, dose selection should be approached with caution. It is generally recommended to start at the lower end of the dosing range, considering the increased likelihood of reduced hepatic, renal, or cardiac function, as well as the presence of concomitant diseases or other drug therapies in this population. Elderly patients may have a higher susceptibility to developing torsades de pointes arrhythmias compared to younger individuals. Additionally, elderly patients undergoing treatment with erythromycin may experience enhanced effects of oral anticoagulant therapy. Erythromycin Delayed-Release Capsules (250 mg) do not contain sodium or potassium. Gender There is no FDA guidance regarding the use of erythromycin in specific gender populations. Race There is no FDA guidance regarding the use of erythromycin in specific racial populations. Renal Impairment There is no FDA guidance on the use of erythromycin in patients with renal impairment. Hepatic Impairment There is no FDA guidance on the use of erythromycin in patients with hepatic impairment. Females of Reproductive Potential and Males There is no FDA guidance on the use of erythromycin in women of reproductive potential or in males. Immunocompromised Patients There is no FDA guidance on the use of erythromycin in immunocompromised patients. Administration and Monitoring Administration: Erythromycin is administered orally. Monitoring: Limited information is available regarding the monitoring of erythromycin in the drug label. IV Compatibility Limited information is available regarding the IV compatibility of erythromycin in the drug label. Overdosage Acute Overdose: In cases of overdose, erythromycin should be discontinued immediately. Management involves the prompt elimination of any unabsorbed drug and the implementation of other appropriate measures. Erythromycin is not removed by peritoneal dialysis or hemodialysis. Chronic Overdose: Limited information is available regarding chronic overdose of erythromycin in the drug label. Pharmacology Mechanism of Action: Erythromycin inhibits protein synthesis by binding to the 50S ribosomal subunits of susceptible organisms. It does not interfere with nucleic acid synthesis. Structure: Erythromycin Delayed-Release Capsules contain enteric-coated pellets of erythromycin base for oral administration. Each capsule contains 250 mg of erythromycin base. Inactive ingredients include cellulosic polymers, citrate ester, D&C Red No. 30, D&C Yellow No. 10, magnesium stearate, and povidone. The capsule shell contains FD&C Blue No. 1, FD&C Red No. 3, gelatin, and titanium dioxide. Erythromycin is produced by a strain of Saccharopolyspora erythraea (formerly Streptomyces erythraeus) and belongs to the macrolide group of antibiotics. The base form is microbiologically active and readily forms salts with acids. Pharmacokinetics Orally administered erythromycin base and its salts are readily absorbed in their microbiologically active form. However, interindividual variations in absorption are observed, and some patients may not achieve adequate serum levels. Erythromycin is largely bound to plasma proteins, with approximately 90% of the absorbed drug being in the freely dissociating bound fraction. After absorption, erythromycin diffuses readily into most body fluids. In the absence of meningeal inflammation, low concentrations are typically achieved in the spinal fluid, but the drug's passage across the blood-brain barrier increases in meningitis. Erythromycin is excreted in human milk and crosses the placental barrier, although fetal plasma levels are low. The drug is not removed by peritoneal dialysis or hemodialysis. In patients with normal hepatic function, erythromycin is concentrated in the liver and excreted in the bile. The effect of hepatic dysfunction on biliary excretion of erythromycin is unknown. After oral administration, less than 5% of the administered dose is recovered in the active form in the urine. The enteric coating of pellets in Erythromycin Delayed-Release Capsules protects the erythromycin base from inactivation by gastric acidity. The small size and enteric coating of the pellets allow them to pass intact from the stomach to the small intestine, where they dissolve efficiently for uniform absorption. Optimal stability in the presence of gastric secretions and complete absorption are achieved when erythromycin is taken on an empty stomach. Mechanism of Resistance The primary mechanism of resistance to erythromycin involves modification of the 23S rRNA in the 50S ribosomal subunit, rendering it insensitive. Efflux mechanisms may also contribute significantly to resistance. Interaction with Other Antimicrobials In vitro antagonism has been observed between erythromycin and clindamycin, lincomycin, and chloramphenicol. Spectrum of Activity Erythromycin has demonstrated activity against the following organisms in vitro and in clinical infections: Gram-positive bacteria: Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Corynebacterium minutissimum, Listeria monocytogenes, Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes. Gram-negative bacteria: Bordetella pertussis, Haemophilus influenzae, Legionella pneumophila, Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Other microorganisms: Chlamydia trachomatis, Entamoeba histolytica, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Treponema pallidum, Ureaplasma urealyticum. Susceptibility Testing When available, clinical microbiology laboratories should provide in vitro susceptibility test results for antimicrobial drugs used in resident hospitals. These periodic reports should describe the susceptibility profile of nosocomial and community-acquired pathogens, aiding physicians in selecting appropriate antibacterial drugs for treatment.
